title: 2 Samuel 6:1–11
context: 2 Samuel 6:1–11 tells of David’s first attempt to bring the ark to Jerusalem. The ark, called by the name of the LORD of Armies who sits above the cherubim, is placed on a new cart, with great music and celebration. When the cattle stumble, Uzzah reaches out and takes hold of the ark, and God strikes him dead. The law required the ark to be carried on poles by the Levites and warned that even the Kohathites must not touch the holy things (Numbers 4:15; compare 1 Chronicles 15:13–15). David is angry and afraid, and he leaves the ark at the house of Obed-Edom, which the LORD blesses. Both traditions read the passage as a sober lesson about God’s holiness and the need to approach him on his terms. Both feel the shock of the judgment, and neither treats the method of transport as a point of division between them.

verses.text: David again gathered together all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: David gathers the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand. Arminians see David bringing the whole nation into the effort to bring the ark to Jerusalem, a public act intended to unite Israel around the worship of the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the large gathering shows the importance David placed on the ark. Both traditions read the verse as the beginning of David’s desire to put God’s presence at the center of his kingdom.

verses.text: David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baale Judah, to bring up from there God’s ark, which is called by the Name, even the name of the LORD of Armies who sits above the cherubim.
verses.arminianNotes: David goes to Baale Judah to bring up God’s ark, called by the name of the LORD of Armies who sits above the cherubim. Arminians see the ark’s title stressing that it represents the presence and authority of God himself, which raises the stakes of how it is handled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Baale Judah is generally identified with Kiriath Jearim, where the ark had rested (1 Samuel 7:1–2; 1 Chronicles 13:6). Both traditions see the description of God enthroned above the cherubim as preparing for the lesson about holiness that follows.

verses.text: They set God’s ark on a new cart, and brought it out of Abinadab’s house that was on the hill; and Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, drove the new cart.
verses.arminianNotes: They set God’s ark on a new cart and bring it out of Abinadab’s house, with Uzzah and Ahio driving. Arminians note that the cart follows the method the Philistines used (1 Samuel 6:7) rather than the law’s instruction to carry the ark on poles (Numbers 4:15; 7:9).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the new cart as a well-intended but improper method, which 1 Chronicles 15:13–15 later identifies as the problem. Both traditions read the detail as preparing for the judgment that follows, and neither divides over it.

verses.text: They brought it out of Abinadab’s house which was in the hill, with God’s ark; and Ahio went before the ark.
verses.arminianNotes: They bring the ark out of Abinadab’s house on the hill, and Ahio goes before it. Arminians see the procession beginning with care and honor, yet still without the proper method God had given for carrying his ark.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The verse repeats part of 6:3, and interpreters note that the Hebrew may contain a copying repetition. Both traditions read it as a narrative detail that builds the scene without adding new doctrine.

verses.text: David and all the house of Israel played before the LORD with all kinds of instruments made of cypress wood, with harps, with stringed instruments, with tambourines, with castanets, and with cymbals.
verses.arminianNotes: David and all Israel celebrate before the LORD with instruments of cypress wood, harps, stringed instruments, tambourines, castanets, and cymbals. Arminians see sincere joy in worship and see the scene as genuine devotion, which makes what follows more striking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the parallel in 1 Chronicles 13:8 reads "with all their might" and "with songs." Both traditions read the verse as showing that enthusiasm in worship does not replace obedience to what God has said.

verses.text: When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reached for God’s ark and took hold of it, for the cattle stumbled.
verses.arminianNotes: At the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reaches out and takes hold of God’s ark when the cattle stumble. Arminian readers see an act that seems instinctive and protective, and they acknowledge the difficulty readers feel at the judgment that follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise feel the weight of the moment. Both traditions read the act in light of the law forbidding anyone, even the Kohathites, to touch the holy things (Numbers 4:15). They see the problem as approaching God’s holiness on human terms, beginning with the cart.

verses.text: The LORD’s anger burned against Uzzah, and God struck him there for his error; and he died there by God’s ark.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s anger burns against Uzzah, and God strikes him there for his error, and he dies by the ark. Arminians read the judgment as a sober display of God’s holiness at a foundational moment for Israel’s worship, not as God acting arbitrarily.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that God’s holiness is not safe to handle carelessly, even with good intentions. Both traditions acknowledge the difficulty of the verse, read it as shared ground about holiness, and note that the word translated "error" is uncertain in Hebrew.

verses.text: David was displeased because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah; and he called that place Perez Uzzah to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: David is displeased because the LORD broke out against Uzzah, and he names the place Perez Uzzah, which the WEB footnote explains means "outbreak against Uzzah." Arminians see honest human emotion in David’s reaction, which the text records without condemnation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note the link with Baal Perazim in 5:20, where the LORD broke out against David’s enemies. Both traditions see the same divine power that saves also judging irreverence, and both read David’s anger as part of a process that leads him to learn.

verses.text: David was afraid of the LORD that day; and he said, “How could the LORD’s ark come to me?”
verses.arminianNotes: David is afraid of the LORD that day and asks how the LORD’s ark can come to him. Arminians see fear turning David to question his approach, an honest response that leads to seeking the right way to worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the fear as an appropriate awareness of God’s holiness. Both traditions read David’s question as a turning point that leads to the proper method in 6:12–15 and 1 Chronicles 15.

verses.text: So David would not move the LORD’s ark to be with him in David’s city; but David carried it aside into Obed-Edom the Gittite’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: David refuses to move the ark to his city and leaves it at the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite. Arminians see David pausing out of caution rather than pressing ahead, and they note that God’s presence is placed in an unexpected household.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. "Gittite" usually means someone from Gath, and some interpreters link Obed-Edom with the Levites named in 1 Chronicles 15–16 and 26:4, though this is debated. Both traditions avoid deciding more than the text allows.

verses.text: The LORD’s ark remained in Obed-Edom the Gittite’s house three months; and the LORD blessed Obed-Edom and all his house.
verses.arminianNotes: The ark remains in Obed-Edom’s house three months, and the LORD blesses him and all his household. Arminians see that God’s presence brings blessing to those who receive it rightly, a contrast with the judgment on Uzzah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the blessing showing that God’s holiness is not hostile to his people when they honor him. Both traditions read the verse as showing that the ark represents blessing as well as danger, depending on how God is approached.
